raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old Caucasian, homosexual male with known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for the past 15 years presented with a disseminated skin eruption over 6 weeks. The patient had been without antiretroviral medications for the past 8 years, defaulted on follow-up, and was uncertain of his last CD4 count or viral load.
The eruption was composed of annular, scalene papules and plaques, some of which were ulcerated (Figure 1). Lesions were distributed on the trunk, extremities, and face. A few lesions demonstrated a thick, ostraceous crust consistent with the skin eruption described in "malignant" syphilis.
Constitutional symptoms included night sweats, decreased appetite, and fatigue. The patient also complained of joint pains at both hands and feet. He denied recent travel, walks in the woods, and recent environmental changes. He could not recall any sick contacts.
Of note, he was allergic to penicillin. The allergy was ascribed since childhood and he could not recall the specific reaction but did emphasize that he was strongly advised against taking any penicillin-containing antibiotics. He denied recent sexual interaction but stated that he contracted HIV via anal intercourse.
The patient looked unwell on general examination. He had pink, but dry mucous membranes and was mildly tachycardic with otherwise unremarkable vital signs. White, adherent plaques were noted in the mouth. The diffuse skin eruption was noted as above. Joint swelling and tenderness were also noted at the wrist and ankles. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were noncontributory.
Initial hematologic workup was significant for mild pancytopenia, leukocyte count 3.4 x 103/mm3, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and platelet count 123 x 103/mm3. The CD4 count was 57 cells/muL and HIV RNA was 365,000 copies/mL. Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor assays were both negative.
Evaluation for additional sexually transmitted infections revealed a negative acute hepatitis panel but a positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) with a titer of 1 : 64. Confirmatory testing with Treponema pallidum antibody (TP-PA) testing was positive. A call to the department of health confirmed no previously reported syphilis infection. Subsequent lumbar puncture was not consistent with infection, specifically a negative VDRL. Blood cultures and wound swabs were negative, and the sedimentation rate was 132 mm/hr.
Punch biopsies were performed on the skin lesions at the left forearm and the left thigh. The histopathologic features were those of psoriasiform lichenoid dermatitis, typical for secondary syphilis. Plasma cells were not readily identified in the infiltrate. Because of the concern for syphilis, a modified Steiner stain was performed which demonstrated several spirochetes within the epidermis.
Plain radiography of the hands and feet revealed polyostotic cortical irregularities of the right foot and both hands, without joint involvement. Roentgenogram of the legs and forearms demonstrated cortical irregularities of the ulnar and radial diaphyses and of the tibial and fibular diaphyses, bilaterally (Figure 2). Roentgenogram of the skull was negative for bony lesions. Follow-up bone scintigraphy was impressive for bilateral, extensive polyostotic uptake within the hands, feet, forearms, and tibiae/fibulae (Figures 3(a)-3(e)).
Based on the positive serology and bone imaging findings, the patient was diagnosed with secondary syphilis osteitis and also now with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
Given his penicillin allergy, the decision was made to treat the patient with an oral regimen: doxycycline 100 mg twice per day for a total of 6 weeks. He commenced receiving Atovaquone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. Prior to discharge (hospital course, day 8), a repeat RPR was performed, with a declining titer of 1 : 32.
The patient was subsequently referred to a HIV clinic where he commenced antiretroviral therapy with Darunavir/Cobicistat, Dolutegravir, and Tenofovir/Emtricitabine. He had one additional follow-up with the HIV clinic and was noted to be compliant with the medications and tolerating them well. He was followed up by his primary care provider at 2 and 6 weeks. During and upon completion of the course of doxycycline, the patient noted considerable improvement in bone pains and joint swelling, which was corroborated on physical examination. At this time, the skin eruption was completely resolved (Figure 4). A follow-up blood count revealed an improvement in the cytopenias. The patient was referred for repeat imaging and RPR titers but defaulted on additional follow-up. Multiple attempts at communication were unsuccessful, and the patient is yet to return to either the HIV clinic or his primary care provider.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old male presenting with a widespread ulcerating skin eruption for six weeks, accompanied by joint pain, night sweats, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-week history of a progressively spreading cutaneous eruption over his face, trunk, and extremities that developed ulcerated and heavily crusted plaques. He concurrently experienced worsening constitutional symptoms including drenching night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, and bilateral joint pains involving both hands and feet. He reported no recent travel, outdoor exposures, or sick contacts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for 15 years, off antiretroviral therapy for the past 8 years due to loss to follow-up; contracted via anal intercourse. Childhood penicillin allergy with strict recommendation to avoid penicillin-containing antibiotics.
subjective.review_of_systems: Constitutional night sweats, fatigue, decreased appetite, joint pains in hands and feet; denies fever, visual symptoms, headache, or genital chancres.

objective.physical_examination: General: Ill-appearing, mildly tachycardic, vitals otherwise unremarkable. HEENT: Pink but dry mucous membranes; adherent white mucosal plaques in the mouth. Dermatologic: Diffuse eruption of annular, scaly papules and plaques with central ulceration and thick, ostraceous crusts across the trunk, extremities, and face. Musculoskeletal: Symmetrical swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists and ankles. Neurologic and cardiopulmonary exams: Noncontributory.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukocytes 3.4 x 10^3/mm3, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelet count 123 x 10^3/mm3 (mild pancytopenia). Inflammatory markers: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 132 mm/hr. Autoimmune serology: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) negative. Infectious serology: Acute hepatitis panel negative; blood cultures and wound swabs negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: Lumbar puncture opening pressure and analysis normal; CSF VDRL negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy (left forearm): Epidermal ulceration with dense dermal lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and endothelial swelling. Skeletal radiography and whole-body bone scintigraphy: Multifocal cortical thickening, periosteal reactions, and increased radiotracer uptake involving the distal radius, ulna, tibia, fibula, and tarsal bones bilaterally, consistent with multifocal osteitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS; CD4 count 57 cells/microL, HIV RNA 365,000 copies/mL) complicated by severe secondary syphilis manifesting as malignant syphilis (lues maligna), bilateral syphilitic osteitis, and oral candidiasis in a penicillin-allergic patient.
Confirmatory Testing: Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) reactive at a titer of 1:64, confirmed by positive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA); Warthin-Starry silver staining of skin biopsy demonstrated characteristic spirochetes.
Plan & Outcome: Due to documented penicillin allergy, treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks, atovaquone for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, and oral antifungal therapy for thrush. Pre-discharge day 8 RPR declined to 1:32. Antiretroviral therapy was initiated with darunavir/cobicistat, dolutegravir, and tenofovir/emtricitabine. Follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks showed complete resolution of skin lesions, marked improvement in bone pain and joint swelling, and hematologic recovery; the patient subsequently defaulted from ongoing care.
